title: Streaming & Token-by-Token UX
summary: A model generates text one token at a time, but a naive agent waits for the whole response before showing anything — so the user stares at a spinner for seconds. Streaming forwards each token the instant it arrives, cutting perceived latency to the time-to-first-token. You consume the stream as a generator, parse partial output (including partial tool-call arguments) as it fills in, and render incrementally so the interface feels alive even while the model is still thinking.

subtopics.title: Streaming lowers perceived latency, not total time
subtopics.explanation: The model still takes the same wall-clock time to finish, but streaming shows the first token in a few hundred milliseconds instead of after the full generation. Users judge responsiveness by time-to-first-token and by seeing steady progress, not by the final timestamp. This is why every production chat UI streams — it turns a multi-second stall into an experience that feels immediate.
subtopics.example:
import time

# non-streaming: user sees nothing until the end
start = time.time()
full = model.complete(prompt)          # blocks ~4s
print(full)                            # first pixel at t=4.0s

# streaming: user sees the first token almost immediately
start = time.time()
for token in model.stream(prompt):     # yields as it generates
    print(token, end="", flush=True)   # first pixel at t=0.3s
# same total time, far better perceived latency

subtopics.title: A token stream is just an iterable of chunks
subtopics.explanation: Provider SDKs expose streaming as an iterator that yields small event objects: text deltas, tool-call deltas, and a final 'done' event carrying usage metadata. You loop over it, accumulate the pieces you care about, and act on each chunk. Treating the stream as an ordinary iterable is what lets you compose it with the rest of your Python code cleanly.

subtopics.title: Partial output must be parsed as it fills in
subtopics.explanation: If the model is emitting JSON or markdown, each chunk may cut a token in half or leave a bracket unclosed, so you can't json.loads a partial buffer. You either render raw text progressively and parse only at the end, or use a tolerant incremental parser that surfaces fields as they complete. Handling partial state correctly is what keeps a streaming UI from flickering or crashing on half-formed data.

subtopics.title: Tool calls stream too — accumulate the arguments
subtopics.explanation: When a model decides to call a tool, the arguments arrive as a stream of JSON fragments keyed by the call's index, not as one complete object. You concatenate the fragments per tool-call id, then parse the assembled JSON once the tool block closes. Reassembling streamed tool arguments correctly is required before you can ever execute the tool the model requested.

subtopics.title: Wrap streams in a generator-based consumer
subtopics.explanation: A reusable generator that yields user-facing text while quietly accumulating the full message and any tool calls keeps streaming logic in one place. Callers just iterate for the UI, then read the finished state off the generator's return value or a captured object. This generator pattern is what lets streaming plug into an agent loop without scattering buffering code everywhere.

foundations.overview: Language models generate autoregressively — one token conditioned on all the tokens before it — so the full response only exists after the last token. A non-streaming agent buffers that entire response and returns it at once, which means the user waits the whole generation time before seeing a single character. Streaming changes the transport, not the model: the provider forwards each token (as a delta event) the moment it is produced, and your code forwards it onward to the terminal, browser, or next stage. The payoff is perceived latency — time-to-first-token drops to a few hundred milliseconds, and the steady flow of text signals progress even on a long answer. In an agent, streaming applies to more than prose: tool-call arguments also arrive as JSON fragments that you must accumulate per call id before parsing and executing. The main engineering challenge is partial state — a half-arrived chunk is not valid JSON and a mid-word delta is not renderable structure — so you accumulate into a buffer, render raw text progressively, and only parse structured data once a block completes. Packaging all of this behind a generator-based consumer keeps the agent loop clean: callers iterate for the live UI and read the assembled message and tool calls when the loop ends.
foundations.formalDefinition: Streaming is the incremental delivery of a model's output as a sequence of delta events (text deltas, tool-call argument fragments, and terminal metadata) consumed as an iterable, where each event is forwarded or accumulated as it arrives rather than buffered until generation completes.
foundations.whyItMatters: Perceived latency, not total latency, determines whether an agent feels responsive; streaming makes time-to-first-token the metric users experience. It is also a prerequisite for interactive agents — you can render partial answers, cancel early, and reassemble streamed tool calls so the loop can act as soon as arguments are complete.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the model as a person reading you an answer aloud as they think of it. Non-streaming is asking them to write the whole thing silently and hand you the page; streaming is listening as they speak. You can start reacting to the first sentence, but you can't act on a half-finished sentence — so you wait for each clause (a completed JSON block) before treating it as a fact.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Chat UIs that type out answers token by token, coding assistants that render code as it generates, voice agents that begin text-to-speech on the first clause, and agent runtimes that reassemble streamed tool-call arguments to dispatch tools the instant they are complete.
foundations.performanceImpact: Streaming does not reduce total generation time or token cost, but it cuts perceived latency to time-to-first-token and enables early cancellation, which can save tokens when a user stops a wrong answer mid-stream.
commonUseCases: Chat and assistant UIs rendering text token by token
Reassembling streamed tool-call arguments in an agent loop
Early cancellation of long or wrong generations
Voice agents starting TTS on the first completed clause

commonMisconceptions.reality: Total generation time and token cost are unchanged. Streaming only changes when the user sees output — it forwards tokens as they are produced, improving perceived, not actual, latency.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can json.loads the buffer after every chunk.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A partial buffer is almost always invalid JSON. You accumulate and only parse when a block completes, or use a tolerant incremental parser; otherwise you get constant JSONDecodeErrors.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Tool calls arrive as one complete object.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Tool-call arguments stream as JSON fragments keyed by call id. You must concatenate the fragments per call and parse only once the tool block closes before executing.

interactiveExamples.title: Reassembling streamed tool-call arguments
interactiveExamples.explanation: Tool arguments arrive as JSON fragments across several deltas. This consumer accumulates fragments per call id and only parses and dispatches the tool once the tool block closes — the correct way to execute a streamed tool call.

codeLab.title: Build a generator-based stream consumer
codeLab.instructions: Implement consume_stream(stream) that iterates a list of event dicts and (1) yields each text delta's text so a caller can render it live, (2) accumulates all text into a full string, and (3) collects any completed tool calls. Each event is a dict with a 'type' key: 'text' events have a 'text' field, 'tool' events have 'name' and 'args' (already parsed) fields, and a final 'done' event ends the stream. The generator must RETURN a dict {"text": <joined text>, "tools": <list of {name, args}>} via StopIteration so the caller reads the assembled state after iterating. Complete the function so the harness passes.

starter.code:
def consume_stream(stream):
    # TODO: yield each text delta for live rendering,
    # accumulate the full text, and collect completed tool calls.
    # RETURN {"text": ..., "tools": [...]} when the stream ends.
    ...

codeLab.testHarness:
stream = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Let "},
    {"type": "text", "text": "me "},
    {"type": "text", "text": "check."},
    {"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather", "args": {"city": "Paris"}},
    {"type": "done"},
]

gen = consume_stream(stream)
seen = []
try:
    while True:
        seen.append(next(gen))
except StopIteration as stop:
    result = stop.value

assert seen == ["Let ", "me ", "check."], seen
assert result["text"] == "Let me check.", result
assert result["tools"] == [{"name": "get_weather", "args": {"city": "Paris"}}], result
print("all tests passed")
hints: Iterate the events and branch on event['type']; only 'text' events should be yielded for the UI.
Accumulate text into a list and join it at the end; collect tool events into a separate list.
In a generator, `return value` sets StopIteration.value, which the harness reads after the loop finishes.

checkpoints.explanation: Streaming forwards tokens as they are produced, so the first character appears in a few hundred milliseconds. Total generation time and token cost are unchanged — only when the user sees output improves.

checkpoints.prompt: This streaming JSON parser floods the logs with errors. What's wrong?
checkpoints.code:
buffer = ""
for chunk in stream:
    buffer += chunk
    data = json.loads(buffer)   # parse every chunk
    render(data)
options: A partial buffer is invalid JSON, so json.loads raises until the object is complete; you must catch/guard it
chunk must be decoded from bytes
checkpoints.explanation: Most intermediate buffers are incomplete JSON, so json.loads raises JSONDecodeError on nearly every chunk. Accumulate and parse only when the object completes (try/except and render raw text meanwhile), or use a tolerant incremental parser.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this generator's return value hold after iteration?
checkpoints.explanation: A generator's `return` sets StopIteration.value. After exhausting the yields, the next call raises StopIteration carrying 'done:ab', which is the pattern used to expose a stream consumer's assembled result.

checkpoints.codeAfter: e['frag']  # concatenate fragments per call id
checkpoints.explanation: Tool arguments arrive as fragments, so you append each fragment to the running string for that call id with `+=`. Only the full concatenation is valid JSON to parse once the tool block closes.

theory.question: What does streaming a model response actually improve, and what does it not change?
theory.directAnswer: Streaming improves perceived latency by delivering tokens as they are generated, so time-to-first-token drops to a few hundred milliseconds and the user sees steady progress. It does not change total generation time or token cost — the same work happens, just forwarded incrementally instead of buffered.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Streaming is incremental delivery of a model's output as a sequence of delta events consumed as an iterable, forwarded to the UI or next stage as each arrives.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Models generate autoregressively, so the full response only exists after the last token; buffering it makes the user wait the entire generation before seeing anything, which feels unresponsive.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The provider emits text deltas, tool-call argument fragments, and a terminal event; your code loops the stream, forwards text immediately, and accumulates fragments (including tool-call JSON) to act on once a block completes.

theory.whyImportant: Users judge responsiveness by time-to-first-token and visible progress, so streaming is the difference between an agent that feels instant and one that appears frozen for seconds.
theory.realWorldExample: A chat assistant that types its answer out word by word feels immediate even on a four-second generation, whereas the same answer delivered all at once feels like a stall.

followUps.question: Does streaming reduce cost?
followUps.answer: Not directly — token cost is the same. It can save tokens indirectly by letting a user cancel a wrong answer early before the model finishes.

followUps.question: Why can't you parse the buffer as JSON on every chunk?
followUps.answer: Intermediate buffers are almost always incomplete JSON, so parsing raises until the object is complete; you accumulate and parse only when a block closes.

theory.question: How do you handle a tool call that arrives over a streaming API?
theory.directAnswer: The tool name and its argument JSON stream as fragments keyed by the call's id, so you concatenate the fragments per id into a running string and parse it only when the tool block closes. Then you execute the tool with the parsed arguments and feed the result back into the loop.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Streamed tool calls are a series of delta events — a start event with the tool name, several argument fragments, and a stop event — that together describe one tool invocation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model generates tool arguments token by token like any other output, so the runtime receives them as partial JSON that is not individually parseable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You keep a per-call-id buffer, append each argument fragment, and on the stop event run json.loads on the assembled string, then dispatch the named tool and return its observation to the agent loop.

theory.whyImportant: Executing a tool before its arguments are complete would parse invalid JSON or call with missing fields; correct reassembly is a prerequisite for any streaming agent that uses tools.
theory.realWorldExample: A weather agent receives '{"ci', then 'ty": "Par', then 'is"}' as separate deltas; only after concatenation does json.loads yield {'city': 'Paris'} to call the tool.

followUps.question: What if two tool calls stream interleaved?
followUps.answer: Key the accumulator by call id (or index), so each call's fragments are concatenated into its own buffer independently.

followUps.question: Can you stream the tool's result back too?
followUps.answer: Yes — after executing, you append the observation and resume the loop, and the model's next response streams like any other.

scenario.question: Your chat agent streams fine for plain answers, but when it returns markdown tables the UI flickers and sometimes renders broken HTML mid-stream. How do you fix it while keeping streaming?
scenario.directAnswer: Separate the transport from the render: keep streaming raw text into a buffer for perceived speed, but only re-parse the buffer into structured markdown/HTML on safe boundaries (e.g., completed lines or blocks) rather than on every token. Render incomplete structures as plain text until they close, so the user still sees progress without half-formed markup.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A partial-output rendering problem where structured content is being parsed from an incomplete buffer on every delta.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A mid-stream buffer can contain a half-open table row or unclosed formatting, so parsing it as complete markdown produces broken or churning output.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You accumulate deltas, detect completed units (a full line, a closed code fence, a finished table), and only promote those to structured rendering, showing everything after the last safe boundary as raw text.

scenario.whyImportant: It preserves the responsiveness win of streaming while avoiding the flicker and broken-markup that come from treating partial output as final, which is a common production polish issue.
scenario.realWorldExample: An assistant rendered each token through a markdown parser and flashed broken tables; switching to line-boundary parsing (structured for completed lines, raw for the trailing partial line) removed the flicker with no latency cost.

followUps.question: Would buffering until the end be simpler?
followUps.answer: Yes but it discards the streaming benefit entirely; boundary-based rendering keeps perceived speed while staying visually stable.

followUps.question: How does this apply to streamed JSON?
followUps.answer: Same idea — render raw text as it streams and only parse into an object once the JSON block is complete, or use a tolerant incremental JSON parser.

coding.question: Write a stream consumer that yields text deltas for live rendering while accumulating the full text and any completed tool calls, exposing the assembled result via the generator's return value.
coding.thoughtProcess: The UI needs each text delta immediately, so I yield text events as they arrive. The agent loop needs the finished message and tool calls afterward, so I accumulate text into a list and collect tool events, then use a generator return so StopIteration.value carries the assembled dict. Branching on an event 'type' key keeps text, tool, and terminal events cleanly separated.
lineByLine: text_parts and tools accumulate the two kinds of state the caller needs after the stream ends.
For a 'text' event we both append to the buffer and yield it so the UI renders it immediately.
For a 'tool' event we record the finalized name and args without yielding, since tools are not user-facing text.
The 'done' event breaks the loop cleanly rather than relying on the iterable simply ending.
`return {...}` sets StopIteration.value, the idiomatic way to hand a generator's final result back to the caller.
The __main__ block shows a caller iterating for live output; the assembled dict is available once iteration stops.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the number of stream events; each is handled once.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(m) for the accumulated text plus collected tool calls.

followUps.question: How would you support streamed tool arguments here?
followUps.answer: Add a per-id buffer that concatenates argument fragments and parse it on the tool's stop event before appending to tools.

followUps.question: How do you let a caller cancel mid-stream?
followUps.answer: Have the caller stop iterating (or send a cancel flag the loop checks); the generator's finally block can then close the underlying provider stream.

keyTakeaways: Streaming forwards tokens as they generate, cutting perceived latency to time-to-first-token without changing total time or cost.
Consume a stream as an iterable of delta events: forward text immediately, accumulate the rest.
Never json.loads a partial buffer — render raw text as it streams and parse structured data only when a block completes.
Tool-call arguments stream as JSON fragments keyed by call id; concatenate per id and parse only on the tool's stop event.
Wrap streaming behind a generator-based consumer that yields UI text and returns the assembled message and tool calls.
